title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Write with an active approach, using sources to build your own argument rather than only reporting them.

title: Two ways to use the same sources
body: Two students can read exactly the same sources and still write very differently. The difference is not how much they read. It is whether they report what others found, or use it to build a position of their own.

title: The passive approach, named
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.123-127) describe one exemplar this way: 'This exemplar illustrates what we call the passive approach to engaging with discourse. Susie has done what many new or less experienced students do when writing: she's prioritised reporting to the reader all the different interpretations she's found ahead of presenting her own view.' Reporting is not the same as arguing.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two draft paragraphs on the same topic, built from the same three sources.

{{learner-a}} writes a paragraph that reports what three sources each say, one after another, and ends without stating a view.

{{learner-b}} writes a paragraph on the same three sources, but opens with the position they are building toward, and uses each source to support or complicate that position.

Both paragraphs cited the same sources. Only {{learner-b}}'s paragraph was actually arguing something.

title: Why reporting is not enough
body: A passive paragraph can be accurate, well-referenced, and still say nothing of its own. An active paragraph uses the same sources in service of a position the reader can agree or disagree with.

displayTitle: Signals of a passive or active paragraph
body: The same sources can be used two different ways. These signals show which way a paragraph is leaning.
instruction: Select each tab to see what to look for.

_items.title: Reporting language
_items.body: Phrases like 'Smith found that...' or 'according to Jones...' repeated across a paragraph, with no sentence that states what you think.

_items.title: Source-led ordering
_items.body: Paragraphs that move source by source, in the order you read them, rather than by the point being made.

_items.title: Positioning language
_items.body: Phrases like 'this suggests...' or 'taken together, these indicate...' that use sources to build toward your own claim.

instruction: Select a highlighted phrase to see what it signals.

_passage.text: Smith (2019) found X, and Jones (2020) found Y
_passage._note: Two findings reported one after another, with nothing yet said about how they relate to the writer's own view.
A third finding added to the list; still no position of the writer's own.

_passage.text: . Taken together, these three studies suggest that the effect depends on context more than either Smith or Jones allowed for
_passage._note: This is the move that turns reporting into positioning: a claim the writer is making, built from, not instead of, the sources.

title: Writing actively from here
body: Before you write a paragraph, decide the position it is building toward. Then bring each source in to support, complicate, or challenge that position, rather than listing what each one separately found.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Find a paragraph you have written recently. Was it reporting sources, or using them to argue something of your own?
What is one sentence you could add to turn a reporting paragraph into a positioning one?
